speaker: Jennifer Doudna
title: Editing Your DNA, with Nobel Prize Winner Dr. Jennifer Doudna
question: In in vivo gene editing, why has the liver been the primary early organ targeted by clinical trials?
guest: The liver is an organ that naturally filters toxins in our body, so a lot of molecules end up in the liver quite naturally. It's a unique organ in that regard, which meant that in the early days of CRISPR, before there were many strategies for delivery, people recognized the liver would be a great organ to target because it very naturally accumulates molecules, including CRISPR. That's been the basis for this ongoing trial. They're using little greasy blobs known as lipid nanoparticles. These are familiar to anyone who had the COVID vaccine because that's how the vaccine is delivered, and those particles naturally traffic to the liver in the body and carry along other molecules like CRISPR.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer: The liver has been the primary early target for in vivo gene editing for several practical and biological reasons. First, delivery is comparatively easy: lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) injected into the bloodstream naturally accumulate in the liver, because hepatocytes express abundant LDL receptors that take up the particles once they're coated with ApoE. This gives efficient, well-characterized uptake without needing novel targeting. Second, the liver is a major production center for secreted and metabolic proteins, so correcting or knocking down a single hepatic gene can treat systemic diseases—examples include transthyretin amyloidosis (CRISPR-based NTLA-2001) and familial hypercholesterolemia via PCSK9 editing. Third, hepatocytes are relatively amenable to editing and the organ's biology, blood supply, and regeneration are extensively studied, lowering scientific risk. Fourth, many monogenic disorders with clear targets (hemophilia, metabolic enzyme deficiencies) are liver-based. Finally, decades of prior liver-directed gene therapy experience provided safety data and manufacturing know-how. Together, easy delivery, systemic therapeutic reach, and abundant well-understood disease targets made the liver the logical proving ground before tackling harder-to-reach tissues.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: The liver has dominated early *in vivo* gene editing trials primarily because its anatomy and physiology make systemic delivery uniquely accessible. Receiving roughly a quarter of cardiac output, the liver features fenestrated sinusoidal capillaries lacking a continuous basement membrane, allowing intravenously infused lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and viral vectors to pass directly from the bloodstream to hepatocytes. Standard LNPs also naturally bind circulating apolipoprotein E, driving efficient, receptor-mediated hepatocyte uptake via low-density lipoprotein receptors without requiring engineered targeting ligands. Beyond delivery, the liver is the site of numerous well-characterized genetic diseases—such as transthyretin amyloidosis, hereditary angioedema, and familial hypercholesterolemia—that can be treated through straightforward gene knockout rather than complex sequence insertion. Because hepatocytes secrete these target proteins into the bloodstream, clinicians can easily quantify editing efficacy through routine, non-invasive blood tests instead of tissue biopsies. Finally, the liver’s relatively tolerogenic immune microenvironment helps dampen inflammatory responses to foreign editing components, further lowering the safety threshold for pioneering systemic therapies.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: The liver has been the primary early target for in vivo gene editing largely because of accessibility and biology. Hepatocytes naturally take up lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which concentrate in the liver after intravenous injection, so no complex targeting is needed—LDL-receptor and ApoE-mediated uptake delivers the editing machinery efficiently. The liver is also highly vascularized, making delivery straightforward. Many metabolic and secreted-protein disorders originate there, so editing hepatocytes can correct conditions like transthyretin amyloidosis, hereditary angioedema, or familial hypercholesterolemia by altering proteins the liver produces. The organ tolerates and regenerates well, and partial editing of a fraction of cells can yield therapeutic benefit, lowering the bar for efficacy. Robust, well-characterized delivery vehicles (both LNPs and AAV serotypes with hepatic tropism) already existed from earlier work. Expression levels and biomarkers (e.g., serum protein concentrations) are easy to measure, enabling clear readouts. Together, these factors—easy delivery, relevant disease biology, regenerative tolerance, and measurable outcomes—made the liver the natural proving ground, exemplified by Intellia's NTLA-2001 TTR program.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
The liver has been the primary early target for in vivo gene editing largely because it is the most accessible internal organ for systemic delivery. When gene-editing cargo is packaged into lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) or adeno-associated virus vectors and infused intravenously, the liver naturally captures most of it. Its high blood flow and porous, fenestrated blood vessels let nanoparticles pass easily from circulation into liver tissue, while LNPs bind apolipoprotein E in the bloodstream to trigger efficient uptake by hepatocytes via low-density lipoprotein receptors.

Beyond delivery, the liver is a central hub for metabolism and secreted plasma proteins, offering high-value clinical targets. Silencing or correcting a single liver gene can treat severe systemic diseases—such as transthyretin amyloidosis, hereditary angioedema, or familial hypercholesterolemia—often using straightforward gene knockout rather than complex gene insertion. Because adult hepatocytes divide slowly, permanent DNA edits remain durable, enabling potentially one-time therapies without overcoming the tighter vascular barriers of organs like the brain or muscle.

models.answer: The liver was an early target for in vivo gene editing because it is relatively easy to reach through the bloodstream and because editing even a fraction of its cells can have a therapeutic effect. Many intravenously administered lipid nanoparticles accumulate in the liver and deliver their cargo to hepatocytes, and some viral vectors also reach these cells efficiently. Hepatocytes make many of the proteins found in blood, so an edit can reduce a harmful protein or restore a missing one, with effects throughout the body. In many cases, a blood test can show whether the edit is having its intended effect.

The liver was an early target because delivery is relatively straightforward and editing some liver cells can benefit the whole body. The liver receives a large share of the blood supply, and its porous capillaries give intravenously administered delivery vehicles access to hepatocytes, the organ’s main functional cells. In some inherited diseases, editing only a fraction of these cells can meaningfully reduce a harmful protein or restore enough of a missing one.
